paragraphs: Every night you lie down, close your eyes and disappear for hours. We spend roughly a third of our lives like this. At first glance that looks like wasted time. In reality, your brain is working flat out during those hours. In the next five minutes you will find out what happens while you sleep, why we get tired and what all of it is good for.

sections.heading: What happens while you sleep
paragraphs: From the outside, sleep looks like a standstill. But the brain does not switch off; it moves through different states. Experts distinguish between non-REM sleep and REM sleep. REM stands for rapid eye movement.

If you measure the brain waves of a sleeping person, these changes are easy to see. In a sleep laboratory they are turned into a kind of map of the night, which shows how a sleeper moves between the stages.

After you fall asleep, you first pass through light sleep, from which you can still wake easily. Then comes deep sleep. Heartbeat and breathing reach their lowest levels, and the brain produces slow, large waves. This is the stage we need in order to feel refreshed in the morning.

About an hour and a half after falling asleep, the first REM sleep begins. Now the brain is almost as active as when you are awake, the eyes dart around under the lids and we dream especially vividly. To stop us acting out our dreams, our arms and legs are temporarily paralysed.

During REM sleep, the thalamus, a kind of relay station in the brain, sends images and sounds to the cerebral cortex. Out of these come the often strange stories of our dreams. We sometimes dream in the other stages too, but usually less vividly.

This cycle repeats several times a night. Early on, deep sleep dominates; towards morning, the REM periods get longer. Brief moments of waking in between are completely normal, and most of the time we don’t even remember them.
This pattern changes with age. Older people spend less time in deep sleep and REM sleep and wake up more often during the night. Short periods of waking, however, are normal at any age.
The pattern of these cycles is the same for almost everyone, even if the exact timing varies. That is why sleep researchers can recognise a healthy night at a glance.

sections.heading: Why we get tired
paragraphs: Two systems decide when we get tired. The first is the internal clock. It sits deep in the brain, in the hypothalamus, and receives information from the eyes about how bright it is. That way it adjusts itself every day to day and night. When it gets dark, the body produces the hormone melatonin, the signal for night time.

The internal clock controls not only sleep but also body temperature and hormones. In the morning it starts the body up before you even wake. The discovery of how this clock works inside our cells won the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

The second system works like an hourglass. As long as you are awake, a substance called adenosine builds up in the brain. The more of it there is, the greater the sleep pressure. During sleep it is broken down again.

Caffeine works exactly at this point. It occupies the docking sites for adenosine and so masks the tiredness. The sleep pressure does not disappear, though. It comes back as soon as the effect wears off.

When the internal clock and daily life fall out of step, you notice it quickly. After a flight across several time zones, your internal clock still says it is day, even though it is night outside. That is the familiar feeling of jet lag.
In the evening the two systems work together. Sleep pressure is high by then, and the internal clock’s wake-up signal fades. That is when you get tired and fall asleep.

If you stay awake for too long, you cannot ignore sleep pressure forever. Eventually you get brief, unintended moments of sleep that can last a few seconds. Behind the wheel of a car, that is dangerous.
So getting tired in the evening is not a sign of weakness. It is simply your body’s two timekeepers doing their job.

sections.heading: What sleep is good for
paragraphs: Sleep is more like a night shift than a break. The brain takes care of several jobs at once. Two of them have been studied particularly well, and both help explain why a good night makes such a difference.
During sleep the brain consolidates memories. What you learned during the day is apparently replayed and stored for the long term. That is why some things come more easily the next morning.

The brain also cleans up. In 2013, researchers at the University of Rochester discovered in mice that during sleep, fluid flows through the brain tissue and flushes out waste products. This cleaning system was almost ten times more active during sleep than while the mice were awake.

These results come from animal experiments. Whether the cleaning system works just as strongly in humans is still being studied. Early studies suggest that in our brains, too, fluid washes through in waves during deep sleep.

How much sleep do we need? Two major sleep medicine societies recommend that adults regularly sleep at least seven hours a night. People who regularly sleep less have a higher risk of conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes and depression. A single short night, on the other hand, is not a problem. Needs also vary a little from person to person.
Besides duration, quality matters too. Regular sleeping times and undisturbed sleep are more restful than long nights that are often interrupted.
Why sleep evolved in the first place, and why we dream, are questions that science has not yet fully answered. Researchers are still working on both.
One thing is certain, though: sleep is not lost time but one of the most important things our bodies do.

keyTakeaways: Sleep is not a standstill but an active state in which the brain moves through several stages.
Two systems make us tired: the internal clock and a sleep pressure that builds with every waking hour.
During sleep the brain consolidates memories and clears away waste, and adults are advised to sleep at least seven hours.

paragraphs: Why do we spend about a third of our lives lying unconscious in bed? From an evolutionary point of view, that is surprising, because a sleeping animal is vulnerable. And yet every human sleeps, and without sleep we quickly feel terrible. Over the next ten minutes you will learn what sleep actually is, what makes us tired, how a night unfolds and how much sleep adults need.

sections.heading: What sleep actually is
paragraphs: From the outside, sleep looks like a standstill. The muscles relax, breathing becomes calm and we barely react to sounds. But the brain does not switch off; it switches modes. Some areas become calmer, while others are especially active.

If you measure the brain’s electrical activity, you can see just how much is going on at night. Over the course of a night we switch several times between light sleep, deep sleep and so-called REM sleep, in which we dream most vividly. The thalamus, a kind of relay station for sensory information, damps down signals from outside during most stages. That is how we manage to tune out the world around us.
Even newborns follow this pattern, just with much more sleep spread across many short stretches of the day. With age, sleep tends to become lighter and more broken up.

Every human sleeps, and a great many animals have sleep-like periods of rest too, right down to fruit flies. From an evolutionary point of view that is remarkable. A sleeping creature does not look for food and is almost defenceless against predators. If sleep has nevertheless won out everywhere, it must be very important.

Learning benefits from sleep too. What you experienced and learned during the day is apparently replayed at night and transferred to other parts of the brain, where it is stored more safely for the long term. At the same time, unimportant connections are weakened, which leaves room for new things. Pulling an all-nighter before an exam therefore tends to do more harm than good.

Today we know that many jobs get done at the same time during sleep. The brain consolidates what we learned during the day and processes emotions. In mice, researchers have also discovered that the brain flushes out waste during sleep. A dedicated cleaning system, the glymphatic system, was almost ten times more active during sleep than while awake.

How important all this is becomes obvious when sleep is missing. After just one short night, concentration and mood suffer and mistakes happen more easily. If sleep stays too short for a long time, the risk of a whole range of diseases goes up. Why sleep originally evolved, however, is still not exactly known.

Sleep is therefore neither a luxury nor a weakness but a basic need, like eating and drinking. It is just as much a part of a healthy life as diet and exercise, and it cannot be cut short at will without us noticing the consequences.
In the next sections you will find out what makes us tired in the evening, how a night is structured and how much sleep adults actually need according to current research.

sections.heading: The two timekeepers
paragraphs: Why do you get tired in the evening and wake up in the morning? Behind this are two systems that work together. One is the internal clock, known as the circadian rhythm. The other is sleep pressure, which experts call sleep-wake homeostasis.

You can picture the two systems as two curves that rise and fall over the course of the day. When you fall asleep and when you wake up depends on how they line up at any given moment. Let’s look at each of them in turn.

The internal clock sits in a tiny area of the hypothalamus, deep in the brain. It is called the suprachiasmatic nucleus and consists of a few thousand nerve cells. It receives information straight from the eyes about how bright it is outside. That way it resets itself every day to the cycle of day and night.

This clock does not just time our sleep. It also influences body temperature, hormones and metabolism. One important signal is the hormone melatonin. It is produced in the pineal gland as soon as it gets dark and tells the body that it is night. Bright light in the evening holds back its release.

Interestingly, the internal clock keeps running even without daylight. In experiments where people lived for weeks without clocks and without sunlight, they kept a rhythm of roughly one day. It just wasn’t exactly 24 hours long; it was usually a little longer. Without light to set the pace, we would slowly drift out of sync with the day.

The second timekeeper works like an hourglass. As long as you are awake, your cells use energy. One of the by-products is a substance called adenosine. It builds up in the brain and increases sleep pressure. The longer you are awake, the more tired you become. During sleep the adenosine is broken down again, and by morning the hourglass has been reset.

This is where coffee comes in. Caffeine occupies the same docking sites in the brain that adenosine normally binds to. In this way it blocks the signal that says you are tired. The sleep pressure itself does not disappear, though; it is only masked. When the effect wears off, the tiredness often comes back all at once.

In everyday life the two systems work together. In the afternoon, sleep pressure is already fairly high, but the internal clock is still keeping you awake. In the evening its wake-up signal fades, and the built-up sleep pressure takes over. Towards morning the pressure has been cleared, and the internal clock starts the body up again.

When the two fall out of step, you notice it immediately. After a flight across several time zones, your internal clock still says it is day, even though it is night outside. That is jet lag. People who work shifts experience something similar, because their working hours run against their internal clock.

It is also important to know that neither system can be fooled indefinitely. You can fight tiredness for a while with light, movement or coffee. But sleep pressure keeps building and eventually has to be paid off. People who stay awake too long eventually experience brief, unintended moments of sleep, often lasting just a few seconds. Behind the wheel of a car, that can be dangerous.

sections.heading: A night in cycles
paragraphs: Not all sleep is the same. Experts distinguish between two basic types: REM sleep and non-REM sleep. REM stands for rapid eye movement. Non-REM sleep is further divided into three stages, from light to deep.

The first stage is the transition from being awake to being asleep. It lasts only a few minutes. Heartbeat and breathing slow down, the muscles relax and sometimes they twitch briefly. From this light sleep you can be woken very easily.

Even in this light stage, the brain is still partly listening. A familiar voice or your own name is more likely to wake you than an unfamiliar noise of the same volume. The filter that shuts out the world is never completely closed.

In the second stage, body temperature drops and the eyes stop moving. Brain waves slow down but keep showing short bursts of electrical activity. Over the whole night, we spend more time in this stage than in any other.

The third stage is deep sleep. Heartbeat and breathing reach their lowest levels, and the brain produces slow, large waves. Anyone woken from deep sleep is often disoriented for a moment. This is the stage we need in order to feel refreshed in the morning. It occurs mainly in the first half of the night.

About an hour and a half after falling asleep, the first period of REM sleep begins. Now the brain becomes very active again, almost as if it were awake. The eyes dart back and forth under the lids, and breathing and pulse become irregular. This is when we dream most, and most vividly. To stop us acting out our dreams, the muscles of the arms and legs are temporarily paralysed.

Why we dream so vividly in REM sleep has to do with the brain’s activity. The thalamus, which shuts out the outside world during deep sleep, now sends images, sounds and other sensations to the cerebral cortex. Out of these come the often strange stories of our dreams. We sometimes dream in non-REM sleep as well, but usually less vividly.

This sequence repeats several times a night. One cycle takes roughly an hour and a half. Early in the night deep sleep dominates; towards morning the REM periods get longer. So if you wake up early, you mainly miss out on REM sleep, and if you fall asleep late, you tend to miss deep sleep.

Brief periods of waking between cycles are perfectly normal, by the way. Usually we don’t even remember them in the morning. The pattern also changes with age. Older people spend less time in REM sleep and deep sleep and wake up more often during the night.

How your own night unfolds can be measured precisely in a sleep laboratory. There, electrodes on the head and body record brain waves, eye movements and muscle tension. The result is a kind of map of the night called a hypnogram. It shows how you move up and down between the stages over the hours, a bit like a ship riding over waves.

sections.heading: How much sleep we need
paragraphs: Perhaps the most common question about sleep is: how much is enough? The answer depends on age. Babies and toddlers need far more sleep than adults, and teenagers need more too. For adults there is a well-founded recommendation.

In 2015 the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society published a joint statement. Fifteen experts reviewed the existing research for it, several thousand scientific articles in total. Their conclusion: adults between 18 and 60 should regularly sleep at least seven hours a night.

According to these reviews, people who regularly sleep less than seven hours have a higher risk of many problems. These include weight gain, diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease and stroke, as well as depression. The immune system also works less well, people make more mistakes and have more accidents. The word regularly is important: a single short night is no disaster.

Surveys from many countries show how big the problem is. According to the sleep societies, more than a third of adults regularly get too little sleep. Long working days, commuting, screens in the evening or worries that keep people awake are often to blame. In everyday life, sleep quickly becomes whatever is left over once everything else is done.

The experts deliberately did not set an upper limit. More than nine hours can be appropriate for young adults, after a period of sleep deprivation or during illness. Whether very long sleep is harmful in itself is unclear. It is often more a consequence of illness than its cause.

Sleep needs also differ from person to person. Genes, life circumstances and health all play a part. Some people get by with a little less, while others need more. Seven hours is therefore a minimum for most people, not an exact measure for everyone.

Besides duration, quality matters too. According to the sleep societies, healthy sleep also means sleeping at suitable times, as regularly as possible and without disruptions such as pauses in breathing. Eight hours with constant waking is less restful than seven hours in one stretch.

And research shows one more thing: we are often poor judges of our own lack of sleep. People who sleep too little for weeks get used to the feeling and think their performance is normal, even though it drops noticeably in tests. Anyone worried about their sleep should talk to a doctor.

Sleep researchers therefore stress that sleep is just as much a part of a healthy life as diet and exercise. It is not a reward for finished work but a precondition for functioning well the next day. Protecting your sleep is an investment in concentration, mood and health.

keyTakeaways: Sleep is an active state, controlled jointly by the internal clock and by sleep pressure from adenosine.
A night consists of several cycles of light sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep, the stage in which we dream most.
Sleep experts recommend that adults regularly get at least seven hours of sleep per night.

sections.heading: Spring cleaning in the brain
paragraphs: One of the most surprising discoveries in sleep research is only a few years old. It concerns a very practical question: how does the brain get rid of its waste? Every cell produces waste products as it works. In the rest of the body, the lymphatic system takes care of this, but it does not reach into the brain.

For a long time, people had wondered how the brain stays clean at all. It is one of the most active organs in the body and uses roughly a fifth of our energy. A correspondingly large amount of waste is produced. The researchers also found it remarkable that the brain uses hardly less energy during sleep than while awake. So it had to be doing something at night.

In 2012 a team led by the neuroscientist Maiken Nedergaard at the University of Rochester discovered a cleaning system of the brain’s own in mice. In it, cerebrospinal fluid flows along blood vessels through the tissue and flushes waste out. Because glial cells play an important role in the process, the researchers called it the glymphatic system.

A year later came the real sensation. The system works mainly during sleep. In the experiments it was almost ten times more active in sleeping mice than in awake ones. During sleep, the cells in the brain shrank so that the space between them grew by about sixty percent. That allowed the fluid to flow through much more easily.

Among the substances carried away is beta-amyloid. This protein is well known because it builds up in the brain in Alzheimer’s disease. Sleeping mice cleared it significantly faster than awake ones. These findings come from animal experiments. Whether, and how strongly, the cleaning system works the same way in humans is being studied intensively. Later studies have found signs that in people, too, cerebrospinal fluid washes through the brain in rhythmic waves during deep sleep. But many details are still unclear.

The possible link to disease is especially interesting. If the brain cleans up during sleep, poor sleep over many years might contribute to harmful proteins building up. Whether poor sleep is a cause of Alzheimer’s or rather an early sign of it cannot yet be said for certain. Most likely the two influence each other.

Even so, the discovery was a turning point in our understanding of sleep. It offers a very tangible reason why the brain has to switch into a different state at night. Cleaning up while running at full power at the same time apparently doesn’t work well.

Research on the glymphatic system is moving fast. Teams around the world are now investigating what role sleeping position, age or certain medicines play in the night-time clean-up. Many of these results are still preliminary. What is clear, though, is that sleep is far more for the brain than just rest.
Perhaps the old saying that a good night’s sleep clears the mind is more literal than anyone ever imagined.

REM sleep probably plays a role in skills and in linking up what you have learned. The tasks cannot be separated neatly, though.

Sleep helps not only with remembering but also with sorting out. Not every impression of the day is worth keeping. Researchers suspect that unimportant connections between nerve cells are weakened during sleep. That leaves room for new things, and what matters stands out more clearly.

For everyday life this means that if you have a lot to learn, it helps to spread the learning over several days. That gives the brain several nights to sort and consolidate what you have learned. A short nap at midday can also help you remember things better. Long naps in the afternoon, however, can disturb your night-time sleep.
In short, a good night’s sleep is one of the best study aids there is, and it costs nothing at all.

From the outside, sleep looks like a standstill. The muscles relax, breathing slows down and the eyes are closed. We barely react to sounds. But that impression is misleading. If you measure the electrical activity of the brain, a very different picture emerges.

The brain does not switch off during sleep; it switches modes. Some areas become calmer, while others are especially active. The thalamus, for example, a kind of relay station for sensory information, damps down signals from the outside world during most stages of sleep. That is how you manage to tune out the world around you.

How much sleep a person needs changes a great deal over a lifetime. A newborn often sleeps sixteen hours or more a day, spread across many short stretches. Toddlers still need considerably more than adults, and teenagers also need more. Only in adulthood does sleep settle into one long block at night.

From an evolutionary point of view, sleep is actually a puzzle. A sleeping creature cannot look for food, cannot reproduce and is almost defenceless against predators. If such a risky state has nevertheless survived, it must be very important. In fact, sleep-like periods of rest have been found in a great many animals, from mammals and birds to fish and even insects.
Even fruit flies have phases in which they are still, harder to wake and which they make up for if they are kept from resting. That suggests sleep is a very old invention of life.

It is also striking how differently animals sleep. Some marine mammals can apparently sleep with one half of the brain while the other half stays awake and keeps an eye on their surroundings. Other animals sleep in many short bursts throughout the day. What almost all of them have in common is that they cannot do without sleep for long.

Exactly what it is for is still being researched. It does not seem to have a single purpose. Sleep is more like a night shift in which many jobs are done at the same time. The brain processes experiences, consolidates what it has learned and cleans up. The body repairs tissue and regulates hormones.

How important all of this is becomes clear mainly when sleep is missing. After just one short night, concentration and mood suffer and mistakes happen more easily. If sleep stays too short for a long time, the risk of a whole range of diseases goes up.
So sleep is neither a luxury nor a weakness. It is a basic need, like eating and drinking. The following sections look at what controls it, how it unfolds and what exactly happens during those hours.

sections.heading: The two timekeepers
paragraphs: Why do you get tired in the evening and wake up in the morning? Behind this are two systems that work together. One is the internal clock, known as the circadian rhythm. The other is sleep pressure, which experts call sleep-wake homeostasis.

You can picture the two systems as two curves that rise and fall over the course of the day. When you fall asleep and when you wake up depends on how they line up at any given moment. Let’s look at each of them in turn.

The internal clock sits in a tiny area of the hypothalamus, deep in the brain. It is called the suprachiasmatic nucleus and consists of a few thousand nerve cells. It receives information straight from the eyes about how bright it is outside. That way it resets itself every day to the cycle of day and night.

This clock does not just time our sleep. It also influences body temperature, hormones and metabolism. One important signal is the hormone melatonin. It is produced in the pineal gland as soon as it gets dark and tells the body that it is night. Bright light in the evening holds back its release.

Interestingly, the internal clock keeps running even without daylight. In experiments where people lived for weeks without clocks and without sunlight, they kept a rhythm of roughly one day. It just wasn’t exactly 24 hours long; it was usually a little longer. Without light to set the pace, we would slowly drift out of sync with the day.

The second timekeeper works like an hourglass. As long as you are awake, your cells use energy. One of the by-products is a substance called adenosine. It builds up in the brain and increases sleep pressure. The longer you are awake, the more tired you become. During sleep the adenosine is broken down again, and by morning the hourglass has been reset.

This is where coffee comes in. Caffeine occupies the same docking sites in the brain that adenosine normally binds to. In this way it blocks the signal that says you are tired. The sleep pressure itself does not disappear, though; it is only masked. When the effect wears off, the tiredness often comes back all at once.

In everyday life the two systems work together. In the afternoon, sleep pressure is already fairly high, but the internal clock is still keeping you awake. In the evening its wake-up signal fades, and the built-up sleep pressure takes over. Towards morning the pressure has been cleared, and the internal clock starts the body up again.

When the two fall out of step, you notice it immediately. After a flight across several time zones, your internal clock still says it is day, even though it is night outside. That is jet lag. People who work shifts experience something similar, because their working hours run against their internal clock.

It is also important to know that neither system can be fooled indefinitely. You can fight tiredness for a while with light, movement or coffee. But sleep pressure keeps building and eventually has to be paid off. People who stay awake too long eventually experience brief, unintended moments of sleep, often lasting just a few seconds. Behind the wheel of a car, that can be dangerous.

sections.heading: A night in cycles
paragraphs: Not all sleep is the same. Experts distinguish between two basic types: REM sleep and non-REM sleep. REM stands for rapid eye movement. Non-REM sleep is further divided into three stages, from light to deep.

The first stage is the transition from being awake to being asleep. It lasts only a few minutes. Heartbeat and breathing slow down, the muscles relax and sometimes they twitch briefly. From this light sleep you can be woken very easily.

Even in this light stage, the brain is still partly listening. A familiar voice or your own name is more likely to wake you than an unfamiliar noise of the same volume. The filter that shuts out the world is never completely closed.

In the second stage, body temperature drops and the eyes stop moving. Brain waves slow down but keep showing short bursts of electrical activity. Over the whole night, we spend more time in this stage than in any other.

The third stage is deep sleep. Heartbeat and breathing reach their lowest levels, and the brain produces slow, large waves. Anyone woken from deep sleep is often disoriented for a moment. This is the stage we need in order to feel refreshed in the morning. It occurs mainly in the first half of the night.

About an hour and a half after falling asleep, the first period of REM sleep begins. Now the brain becomes very active again, almost as if it were awake. The eyes dart back and forth under the lids, and breathing and pulse become irregular. This is when we dream most, and most vividly. To stop us acting out our dreams, the muscles of the arms and legs are temporarily paralysed.

Why we dream so vividly in REM sleep has to do with the brain’s activity. The thalamus, which shuts out the outside world during deep sleep, now sends images, sounds and other sensations to the cerebral cortex. Out of these come the often strange stories of our dreams. We sometimes dream in non-REM sleep as well, but usually less vividly.

This sequence repeats several times a night. One cycle takes roughly an hour and a half. Early in the night deep sleep dominates; towards morning the REM periods get longer. So if you wake up early, you mainly miss out on REM sleep, and if you fall asleep late, you tend to miss deep sleep.

Brief periods of waking between cycles are perfectly normal, by the way. Usually we don’t even remember them in the morning. The pattern also changes with age. Older people spend less time in REM sleep and deep sleep and wake up more often during the night.

How your own night unfolds can be measured precisely in a sleep laboratory. There, electrodes on the head and body record brain waves, eye movements and muscle tension. The result is a kind of map of the night called a hypnogram. It shows how you move up and down between the stages over the hours, a bit like a ship riding over waves.

sections.heading: Spring cleaning in the brain
paragraphs: One of the most surprising discoveries in sleep research is only a few years old. It concerns a very practical question: how does the brain get rid of its waste? Every cell produces waste products as it works. In the rest of the body, the lymphatic system takes care of this, but it does not reach into the brain.

For a long time, people had wondered how the brain stays clean at all. It is one of the most active organs in the body and uses roughly a fifth of our energy. A correspondingly large amount of waste is produced. The researchers also found it remarkable that the brain uses hardly less energy during sleep than while awake. So it had to be doing something at night.

In 2012 a team led by the neuroscientist Maiken Nedergaard at the University of Rochester discovered a cleaning system of the brain’s own in mice. In it, cerebrospinal fluid flows along blood vessels through the tissue and flushes waste out. Because glial cells play an important role in the process, the researchers called it the glymphatic system.

A year later came the real sensation. The system works mainly during sleep. In the experiments it was almost ten times more active in sleeping mice than in awake ones. During sleep, the cells in the brain shrank so that the space between them grew by about sixty percent. That allowed the fluid to flow through much more easily.

Among the substances carried away is beta-amyloid. This protein is well known because it builds up in the brain in Alzheimer’s disease. Sleeping mice cleared it significantly faster than awake ones. Nedergaard compared it to a party: you can either entertain the guests or clean the house, but you can’t really do both at the same time.

These findings come from animal experiments. Whether, and how strongly, the cleaning system works the same way in humans is being studied intensively. Later studies have found signs that in people, too, cerebrospinal fluid washes through the brain in rhythmic waves during deep sleep. But many details are still unclear.

The possible link to disease is especially interesting. If the brain cleans up during sleep, poor sleep over many years might contribute to harmful proteins building up. Whether poor sleep is a cause of Alzheimer’s or rather an early sign of it cannot yet be said for certain. Most likely the two influence each other.

Even so, the discovery was a turning point in our understanding of sleep. It offers a very tangible reason why the brain has to switch into a different state at night. Cleaning up while running at full power at the same time apparently doesn’t work well.

Research on the glymphatic system is moving fast. Teams around the world are now investigating what role sleeping position, age or certain medicines play in the night-time clean-up. Many of these results are still preliminary. What is clear, though, is that sleep is far more for the brain than just rest.
Perhaps the old saying that a good night’s sleep clears the mind is more literal than anyone ever imagined.

sections.heading: Learning while you sleep
paragraphs: Perhaps you have noticed that something you struggled with the evening before comes more easily the next morning. That is no coincidence. Sleep plays an important role in strengthening memories. Experts call this memory consolidation.

During the day, the brain constantly takes in new impressions. Much of this first ends up in a kind of temporary store, for which the hippocampus is important. During sleep, the day’s experiences apparently get replayed, and important content is transferred to other areas of the cerebral cortex. There it is stored more safely for the long term.

Researchers have observed this very vividly in rats. When the animals ran through a maze during the day, certain nerve cells in the hippocampus fired in a fixed order. During the sleep that followed, the same order appeared again, only much faster. The brain seemed to be going over the route once more in its sleep.

According to current knowledge, this process needs both types of sleep. Deep sleep seems to be particularly important for facts and experiences, the things you can put into words. REM sleep probably plays a role in skills and in linking up what you have learned. The tasks cannot be separated neatly, though.

Sleep helps not only with remembering but also with sorting out. Not every impression of the day is worth keeping. Researchers suspect that unimportant connections between nerve cells are weakened during sleep. That leaves room for new things, and what matters stands out more clearly.

Feelings are processed at night as well. During REM sleep the amygdala is especially active, an almond-shaped area involved in emotions. Many experts think it is possible that sleep helps us put stressful experiences into perspective. It is not for nothing that people say you should sleep on an important decision.

The effect also shows up in reverse when sleep is lacking. People who sleep too little find it harder to concentrate and learn new material less well. Their mood suffers too, and they get irritated more easily. From the point of view of sleep research, cramming through the night before an exam is therefore a poor strategy.

Learning in your sleep through headphones, on the other hand, is a myth. Simply playing new vocabulary at night achieves very little, as far as we know. Sleep mainly helps to consolidate what you have worked on during the day.

For everyday life this means that if you have a lot to learn, it helps to spread the learning over several days. That gives the brain several nights to sort and consolidate what you have learned. A short nap at midday can also help you remember things better. Long naps in the afternoon, however, can disturb your night-time sleep.
In short, a good night’s sleep is one of the best study aids there is, and it costs nothing at all.

sections.heading: How much sleep we need
paragraphs: Perhaps the most common question about sleep is: how much is enough? The answer depends on age. Babies and toddlers need far more sleep than adults, and teenagers need more too. For adults there is a well-founded recommendation.

In 2015 the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Sleep Research Society published a joint statement. Fifteen experts reviewed the existing research for it, several thousand scientific articles in total. Their conclusion: adults between 18 and 60 should regularly sleep at least seven hours a night.

According to these reviews, people who regularly sleep less than seven hours have a higher risk of many problems. These include weight gain, diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease and stroke, as well as depression. The immune system also works less well, people make more mistakes and have more accidents. The word regularly is important: a single short night is no disaster.

Surveys from many countries show how big the problem is. According to the sleep societies, more than a third of adults regularly get too little sleep. Long working days, commuting, screens in the evening or worries that keep people awake are often to blame. In everyday life, sleep quickly becomes whatever is left over once everything else is done.

The experts deliberately did not set an upper limit. More than nine hours can be appropriate for young adults, after a period of sleep deprivation or during illness. Whether very long sleep is harmful in itself is unclear. It is often more a consequence of illness than its cause.

Sleep needs also differ from person to person. Genes, life circumstances and health all play a part. Some people get by with a little less, while others need more. Seven hours is therefore a minimum for most people, not an exact measure for everyone.

Besides duration, quality matters too. According to the sleep societies, healthy sleep also means sleeping at suitable times, as regularly as possible and without disruptions such as pauses in breathing. Eight hours with constant waking is less restful than seven hours in one stretch.

And research shows one more thing: we are often poor judges of our own lack of sleep. People who sleep too little for weeks get used to the feeling and think their performance is normal, even though it drops noticeably in tests. Anyone worried about their sleep should talk to a doctor.

Sleep researchers therefore stress that sleep is just as much a part of a healthy life as diet and exercise. It is not a reward for finished work but a precondition for functioning well the next day. Protecting your sleep is an investment in concentration, mood and health.

sections.heading: A clock in every cell
paragraphs: That living things have an internal rhythm has been known for a long time. Plants open and close their leaves in a daily rhythm, even when they are kept in the dark. How this clock works on the inside, however, long remained a mystery.

The answer was found by three American researchers: Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young. They studied fruit flies and isolated a gene that controls the daily rhythm. The gene contains the blueprint for a protein that builds up in cells over the course of the day and is broken down again at night.

The clever part is a feedback loop. When there is a lot of the protein, it slows down the production of its own blueprint. Then it is gradually broken down, and production starts up again. This creates a cycle that lasts about 24 hours. For this discovery the three received the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

We now know that this mechanism works according to the same basic principles in almost all cells of multicellular organisms, including humans. A large proportion of our genes is regulated by the internal clock. The clock in the hypothalamus acts a bit like a conductor, keeping the many small clocks in the body in time with one another.

The morning is a good example of how all this works together. Even before you wake up, the internal clock starts the body up. Body temperature rises and more of the stress hormone cortisol is released. It helps you become alert and ready for the day. In the evening, temperature falls again and melatonin takes over.

Because the internal clock does not run at exactly 24 hours, it has to be reset every day. The most important signal for this is light, especially in the morning. Researchers call such signals zeitgebers, a German word that has made its way into English. Mealtimes, exercise and social contact also help to set the clock.

Not everyone ticks the same way. Some people are bright and alert early in the morning and tired early in the evening; others only really get going late in the day. These differences are called chronotypes, or larks and owls in everyday language. They are partly inborn and change with age. Teenagers, for example, tend to get tired later.

When daily life and the internal clock are out of step for a long time, it can take its toll. The Nobel committee explicitly pointed out that such a mismatch is associated with a higher risk of various diseases. So the internal clock is more than a curiosity; it affects our health.

Research on the internal clock also has practical consequences. Some medicines work better at certain times of day than at others, because the body processes them differently depending on the hour. This field is called chronomedicine. It is still in its early days, but it could help to match treatments more closely to the body’s rhythm.

sections.heading: What we still don’t know
paragraphs: Despite all the progress, sleep remains one of the great mysteries of biology. The most important open question is also the simplest: why did sleep evolve at all? Cleaning up, learning, saving energy and repair are all good candidates. But nobody knows which job came first.

Perhaps the question is the wrong one. Sleep may have arisen early in evolution for one simple reason and then gradually taken on more and more tasks. One argument for this is that even very simple creatures have periods of rest that resemble sleep.

Dreams are a puzzle too. Every night we spend a lot of time in stages in which we dream vividly. Whether dreams have a function of their own or are more of a by-product of brain activity is debated. Some researchers see them as a kind of rehearsal for difficult situations, others as part of the brain’s night-time memory work. None of these ideas has been fully proven.

Another open question concerns the differences between people. Why do some people cope well with six hours, while others are still tired after eight? Early studies have found rare gene variants linked to a much shorter need for sleep. How common such variants are and what exactly they do, however, is still barely understood.

It is also still open exactly how sleep and health are connected. Many studies show links, for example between short sleep and heart disease. Whether sleep is the cause, or whether both share a third cause, cannot always be untangled in such observational studies. That is why experiments in sleep laboratories are so important.

Finally, the way we sleep is changing. Electric light, screens and flexible working hours keep pushing our daily lives further into the night. What this means in the long run is being studied intensively. Light in the evening can hold back the release of melatonin and shift the internal clock later.

New methods are helping in the search for answers. Modern imaging now makes it possible to watch cerebrospinal fluid flowing through the sleeping human brain. Genetic studies show which genes influence whether someone is more of a lark or an owl. And devices worn on the wrist provide huge amounts of data on everyday sleep, even if they measure far less precisely than a sleep laboratory.

How much sleep the body can make up for is not fully clear either. A few hours of lost sleep can be partly recovered at the weekend. Whether the effects of years of short nights can be completely reversed, however, is not known. Many experts therefore recommend regular sleep rather than long lie-ins at the weekend.

One thing can already be said with certainty, though: sleep is not lost time. It is one of the most important things our bodies do, and research keeps discovering new reasons why it is so indispensable.
Perhaps that is the most fascinating thing about sleep. Something we all do every single night still holds some of the deepest secrets of the brain.

keyTakeaways: Sleep is an active state, controlled by the internal clock and by the sleep pressure that builds up while we are awake.
At night the brain moves through light, deep and REM sleep, consolidates memories and clears away waste.
At least seven hours is considered healthy for adults, but why sleep evolved and why we dream are still not fully understood.
